utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome back. We resume with a witness now for whom there are protective measures, so it will be necessary to go into closed session. While that is happening, could I remind you that because of a Plenary meeting of Judges this afternoon, we must finish at 4.45, which will I think be most conveniently arranged for us sitting for an hour, having the usual break, and then sitting for one further hour to 4.45 when we have the cessation for the day. So it will be a short day. Tomorrow we will now be sitting in the morning. The programming had Judge Baird sitting in two courtrooms at once. He has many skills, he tells me, but he has yet to perfect that one, so he will now be sitting with us in the morning tomorrow morning and in another matter tomorrow afternoon. So just be alert tomorrow morning, you need to wake up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in closed session, Judge

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please start out by stating your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: My name is John Harry Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you're a retired colonel with the British army with some 37 years of experience?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I also understand that you held the position of defence attache at the UK embassy in Belgrade from August 1996 to about 23rd March 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In relation to your work as defence attache of the British government, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution on 30th and 31st October 2006, which refers to your work specifically in the years 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review your statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I have had that chance, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in proofing last week when we met, you indicated that there were some corrections you wanted to make to your statement. In order to proceed efficiently through these corrections, I propose to read them out and have you confirm if the corrections accurately reflect what you believe should be stated in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I wish to indicate, Your Honours, just for the reference of the Court, that these corrections were also made in the Milutinovic case; however, there was some confusion in that case with regard to the dates of certain incidents, and the witness has requested that we correct -- make these corrections once again just for the clarity of the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the first correction concerns paragraph 50 and 51. You indicated in proofing that these paragraphs had been inappropriately merged and that some information which pertained to paragraph 50 was contained in paragraph 51. And I'm going to read out -- paragraph 50 should start out. The first sentence it should read: "On 27th August 1998, I showed Ojdanic photographic evidence of the VJ shelling Suva Reka which had occurred shortly before. His reaction was that force would be met with appropriate force." Is that correct that that paragraph should start out with that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And later on in that same paragraph, this is a sentence that starts with: "Ojdanic had stated that force would be met with force and then I pointed out that on another occasion, I had observed four hours of direct and indirect fire on Dunjic, Prilep, Rznic, and Glodjane which had created a deteriorating security and humanitarian problem. The general agreed with my observations."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now moving on to paragraph 51, you indicated that the first sentence should read: "On approximately 28 September 1998, Lord Ashdown also went to see Mr. Milosevic directly after his visit to Kosovo on one occasion and I believe made comments to Mr. Milosevic regarding the shelling west of Suva Reka and other incidents as referred in the paragraph above." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is also correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And moving on to paragraph 69, and this is towards the bottom of the paragraph, there's a sentence that reads: "There are two extra VJ brigades (211th Brigade from Nis and 1st Armoured Brigade from Belgrade) not seen before deployed in the area of Kursumlija." And you added this phrase: "And an armoured brigade at Raska possibly the 37th Motorised Brigade on the two major approach routes." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- also just for the clarity and for the understanding of the Chamber of this statement, there are a number of exhibits that are referred to in this statement which are referred to as exhibit with a number to be assigned, and I just wish to indicate for the reference of the Chamber what the exhibit numbers in this case are of those exhibits and I'll just -- I'll make reference to the specific paragraph where these are mentioned. The first one is at paragraph 35, line 2, and it's a document dated 5th June 1998, and it parentheses it says, "Exhibit number to be assigned." The 65 ter exhibit number for that document is 02552, and the ERN is indicated in that sentence. The second one is in paragraph 50, line 2. Again what -- there is a reference to an exhibit number to be assigned. The 65 ter exhibit number for a document with ERN R0636194, R0636195 is 02554. A further document is in paragraph 61, line 1. Again, it's referred to an exhibit number to be assigned. The 65 ter exhibit number for that document is 02553. In paragraph 60 there's a reference to an exhibit number 2166. That's an exhibit number from the Milutinovic case, and the exhibit number for that document in this case is P87. Paragraph 73, there's a reference to three operation orders and they're listed with their corresponding ERN numbers. The exhibit number for ERN K0520028 is D105. The exhibit number for K0520036 is P971, and the exhibit number for K0520043 is P970. Finally one last reference to an exhibit, paragraph 14, line 6, incorrectly refers to an exhibit as P2166 and this is an exhibit which are the minutes of a meeting of the Pristina MUP staff of 17 February 1999. That exhibit number should be P85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you proceed, line 25 of 6 you've quoted the number there. I think it should end with 42 rather than 43. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, it's K0520043 -- 42, I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: 42, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is referring to paragraph 73 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm slightly confused by what colleague Kravetz has said because previously she gave me a list which is on the notification, and now we have been given exhibits which are not on the list. Namely, the numbers of the exhibits given on the list and most of them should actually be assigned numbers. Actually does this -- no, I agree in principle with this approach. But this means that all documents that had been used in the Milutinovic case and have -- and were tendered and accepted with this witness would have to be on that list. The Defence has four or five documents which have not been accepted during this case and which were tendered and adopted into the file during the Milutinovic case through this particular witness so that we also intend to tender them for admission into the file, just as the Prosecution is doing, that is if you've understood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say we will shortly -- when Ms. Kravetz is finished identifying the documents she proposes to tender, we will first receive the previous statement as an exhibit. We will then receive each of the exhibits that she tenders being exhibits that were tendered in the course of the earlier trial and are referred to in the statement. And if there are then additional exhibits that you want to tender in the course of your cross-examination, you may do so. We will, I think for convenience, receive now the statement, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And that is fine, Your Honours. I was just going to confirm with the witness that he agreed that the contents of the statement were true and accurate to the best of his knowledge and belief now that these corrections have been made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I do wish to indicate that the documents that my learned colleague is referring to that were not on the notification are documents that we do not intend to use in this -- during the testimony of this witness in these proceedings. I am just indicating the exhibit number of these documents for the ease of reference of the Chamber and the Defence since the statement only refers to them by their ERN number. So I seek to tender the statement, and it's 65 ter 02645.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P01400, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And if you -- when you have finished identifying the statements you -- the exhibits you propose to tender, I will arrange for the Court Officer to assign them numbers and to indicate in a short memo to the parties and to the Chamber the numbers that are assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the start of today's session we provided the Registry and Defence with a list of the exhibits that we propose to tender and with -- and this short list indicates also the paragraph numbers where these exhibit numbers are referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So that has already been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is most helpful. I just see that your last indication of the number at 8 -- page 8, 1, was not complete. It was number Exhibit P1400, as I understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you also previously testify before this Tribunal in the case of Milutinovic et al. in February 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to review the transcript of your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed that transcript, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked during your testimony in that case, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this transcript. We have two versions in the e-court system, a redacted public version, which is 05211, and an under seal unredacted version, which is 0521101. The reason we have two versions is because some -- there was some discussion during the previous testimony of this witness that took place in closed session, so we have redacted that from the public version. And I seek to tender both versions of this transcript into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive, first, the full transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Which is under 65 ter number 0521101 and that will be assigned P1401, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Which is under 65 ter 05211 would be assigned P1402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will now proceed to read the in-court summary for this witness. The witness is a retired British army officer. Between 1996 and March 1999 he was the British military attache at the UK embassy in Belgrade. The witness describes MUP and VJ forces present in Kosovo during his tour of duty. He describes the locations where these forces were seen, their tactics, and the various uniforms, weaponry, and vehicles used. The witness speaks about the escalating tensions between the KLA and Serb forces in 1998, and the operations by Serb forces. The witness travelled throughout Kosovo in 1998 and early 1999, and recounts instances where VJ and MUP forces used excessive and disproportionate force which resulted in wanton damage to civilian property, killed livestock, and looting. The witness describes troop movements throughout 1998 and into 1999. The witness also describes meetings and briefings that he had with various senior Yugoslav military officers in 1998, including General Ojdanic, General Dimitrijevic, and General Perisic. The witness raised complaints with the VJ about the heavy-handed tactics used by VJ units during their operations. The witness speaks about the presence of VJ and MUP units from outside Kosovo after the 1998 October agreements and the build-up of these units in 1999. Specifically, he describes VJ/MUP actions in Podujevo in December 1998 and in Racak in January 1999. Finally, the witness describes the coordination between the MUP and the VJ in combat actions during the 1998 summer offensive and joint operations preceding the NATO 1999 campaign. That is the end of the in-court summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are there any more documents that you propose to tender from the statement or the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose during the course of my examination to go through some documents. These are documents that are referred to in the statement, so they are the -- some of them are on the list -- well, all of them are on the list that have been handed to the Registry this morning and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive those identified documents now. They will become exhibits. Numbers will be assigned and a list will be provided to counsel of those exhibit numbers in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, with the leave of the Court, I would like to hand -- have the usher hand to the witness a list of the -- a hard copy of the documents that we're going to be going through today, just so he can review them and comment on them with greater ease and can refer to them. These are all documents that were listed in our notification. I should also point out that the witness has with him in court today a map. It's his personal map of Kosovo province that he brought with him and he would like the Court's leave to be able to refer to this map should the need arise during the course of his testimony in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will assess that if the need arises.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just pointing it out because the witness has it in front of him, just so you're aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask you to first turn to tab 1 of your bundle of documents. This is the witness statement, the 65 ter 02645.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would ask for page 7 in the English to be displayed. It's page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 28. This is on page 7 of the hard copy that you have before you. In paragraph 28 you refer to having seen, on 5th March 1998, the biggest build-up of MUP forces to date, with over 200 MUP present at a check-point in Komorane, and then you refer to an assault at Donje Prekaz in the compound of the Jashari family, and you mention that you photographed bodies there. Could you just very briefly explain to the Court how it is that you came to be there at the Jashari compound and what was your purpose of your visit to that locality.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: When the tensions began to start in Kosovo, the various NATO Defence Attaches, the American, Canadian, French, Italian, German, Dutch, and the UK decided that they would monitor events in Kosovo in order to report to their respective governments of the situation that was starting to escalate. When the presence of the Kosovo Liberation Army became apparent from 1996 onwards until the scenario you've just been told in Donje Prekaz happened in early 1998, on this particular occasion I was touring with the American defence attache in the knowledge that something had happened in the Drenica area. And therefore, we came from Pristina along the main road towards Pec to the crossroads at Komorane where there was this very large gathering of MUP. We subsequently -- we were not allowed into that area for obvious reasons. We then drove on down to Klina and we came around the north through Rudnik, and the whole area was under severe MUP coverage as this operation commenced. It was sometime later that I secured entry to the area of Donje Prekaz, where the Jashari family home had been quite literally torn apart. We heard from other sources that persons had been taken to Pristina and then bodies were returned to the area dead. These are the bodies that I photographed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you refer to having seen this build-up on the 5th of March, 1998. Was this the first time that you toured Kosovo that year?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the first time, but I think the build up of this particular operation had been initiated by a KLA attack on the police station at Rudnik, and I -- forgive me, I cannot remember but I think two or three MUP were killed and therefore this operation, if you will, was in retaliation for that attack on the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you indicate in that same paragraph that you believed it was the MUP who had carried out the operation and you refer to the JSO and SAJ unit of the MUP having been involved along with the PJP. What was the basis for that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've made many statements to this Court and there are many reports that I made to -- both to my government and back to Belgrade. Those were the details in 1998 which were correct, and I will stand by those reports. So yes, they were those units involved. But we're now talking about some 12 years later and a lot of water has passed under the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, in the next paragraph you indicate - this is paragraph 29 - that on 24th March, you reported the first obvious indications of Serbs building up to conduct a joint strike in the Decani area, and in the next paragraph you also speak about a build-up of the VJ occurring in the Decani area and of VJ forces providing fire support for western Kosovo. Up until that time - and we're talking very early 1998 - what did you understand to be the role of the VJ forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This initial operation, like many counter-insurgency operations, is normally run by the police, in this case the MUP. But it would be disingenuous to say that it was not a combined operation because any operation that is dealing with an internal security situation and particularly bearing in mind that within Kosovo you had 52 Corps with some 15 to 20.000 Vojska Jugoslavije personnel currently stationed in Kosovo itself. So it makes complete sense that there is coordination between the two major security forces, the MUP and the VJ, and that inevitably both would become involved in what became a very complex operation against the Kosovo Liberation Army. In Decani in particular, this was a deployment of artillery, presumably to cover the western area, both out towards Pec in the north and down towards Djakovica in the middle south of the area. Again, it makes reasonable sense. It just shows the possible heavy-handed use of force that was to become very prevalent throughout 1998 and into 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify your answer, you refer to the 52nd Corps. Which unit or which corps specifically are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The 52 Corps is the Pristina Corps, which is part of 3rd Army based in Nis, and in the early days that was commanded by General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: And General Pavkovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, just going back to my question. In these initial visits that you -- or tours that you carried out in Kosovo in 1998, I was asking about what you understood to be the role of the VJ forces in Kosovo based on the information you had as defence attache.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The VJ had basically four roles. As I've indicated to Your Honours that they had permanent presence within the area and therefore they obviously had to protect their own bases, their own exercise areas, the international borders to Albania and Macedonia, and also the lines of communication between those bases throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you see these roles of the VJ in Kosovo change at any time in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, they changed probably in the autumn, in September/October, when it appeared that the MUP required more help to deal with the emerging Kosovo Liberation Army. And there are certain skills that the MUP did not have, in particular they didn't have personnel trained in artillery or in the use of tanks and other heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to this topic later on during my examination. I would just like to move away from your statement and ask you to turn to tab 2 of your bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 00688, if we could have that document displayed on the screen. I would just like to point out, Your Honours, that the document we have on the screen has some redactions. These are redactions that have been made by the Rule 70 provider, and -- in granting us authorisation to use these documents in these proceedings. So all the documents that we will be using today you will see have similar redactions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise this document? We see it's a document that has a subject: Kosovo sitrep, and it's dated 11th/12th May 1998. This is tab 2 of your bundle.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you very briefly explain to the Court what this document is, what it consists of.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: During the period 1998 to 1999, Your Honours, I made about 80 written reports which were sent via Belgrade back to our foreign commonwealth office and also to the Ministry of Defence, and this is one of those what we call situation reports of events that happened on the dates shown at the head of each of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if you turn to the second page under number 7, we see the name Donnelly on the document as the person signing off this document. Could you explain who that is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Ambassador Donnelly was my ambassador during this period, and as part of his team within the British embassy in Belgrade, all my reports were passed through him for his political comment, if that was thought necessary. And as I've stated before, it was a question of myself as the defence attache working in tandem with Ambassador Donnelly on the political side to ensure that we produced the most accurate reports of a very challenging situation that was going on in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you say that you were working in tandem with Ambassador Donnelly on the production of these reports. What was your role in the production of these reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As his defence attache, with my considerable experience, I would give my comments on the military situation, where I thought it might be going, what we could try and do to help the situation, and he would accept that and he would add his political thoughts on the situation from his viewpoint back in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So would it be fair to describe this document that we have here on the screen and that you have before you as a contemporaneous report of the security situation on the ground based on your observations and the information you had at the time? Would that be an accurate description of what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's a very accurate way of stating it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if you could go back to page 1 and I'm interested in paragraph 2, which refers to Ponosevac. I'm just waiting for our electronic system to display that on the screen. Now, you make some observations there about the village of Ponosevac and I would just like to ask you to comment on this, and it's the paragraph that starts: "Road from south to Ponosevac 'carpeted' in empty cases including 40-millimetre grenades."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, the area of Ponosevac is a very isolated village close to the Albanian border which was an MUP station, an area where there was considerable activity both from the KLA and from the MUP security forces. On this particular day when we were down there, the road literally was carpeted with empty shells and there was no sign of any villagers. There had been a lot of structural damage done to the houses by shell fire. There were dead animals in the field and the whole area, as I say, was vacant of any local population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if you could turn to paragraph 7, which is on the second page in the English. It's on page 3 in the B/C/S version of this document and it's a paragraph that has the heading: "Assessment." And it says: "Situation could rapidly spin out of control ..." and the last sentence is what I'm interested in. "Heavy-handed terror action in Ponosevac area indicates that the tactical thought process has not changed." Could you explain what that last sentence refers to or what that comment refers to.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Sadly, throughout the Balkan conflict we have seen very heavy-handed tactics in which -- usually it's innocent civilians that get in the way of the opposing forces and one had hoped that we might have avoided this in Kosovo. Sadly, as you can see from this report, even in the early days we were back to the same shelling and wanton destruction of villages. When I challenged this it was because -- the reason behind it was that the Serbian security forces were clearing the routes of ambush positions by blowing up the houses. All that this creates is a population that may not have been interested in either party being in the area, but after their house had been removed, they certainly weren't going to be signing up for the party that had removed their house. And this was the start of that particular campaign where villages were wantonly damaged and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit is 00688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's on my list of documents, yes -- well -- with further documents I think I'll just indicate that they're on my list of documents so exhibit numbers will be assigned in due course. I think that's easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now move to 65 ter 00687, and this is tab 3 in your bundle of documents. And this is again a report. It's dated 28th May 1998. And if we zoom in on this first page at the bottom, we see that it says: "A two-day tour of western Kosovo," and then there are a series -- and this is under the heading "Summary," a series of observations. Sir, did you participate in this two-day tour of western Kosovo that this report refers to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that this is a much lengthier report than the one we just looked at, it has four pages. Would this report have been compiled in the similar fashion as the first report that we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to turn to page 2, and this is page 2 in the English, the bottom part, and it's page 6 in the B/C/S. And it's number 4 that has a heading: "House burning in villages north of Decani." And if you could tell us about that, what this specific section refers to, this section on house burning in villages north of Decani.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The major road that leads north from Djakovica through Decani, up to the major town of Pec in the north, really became the front line between the KLA, the UCK, and the Serbian forces. And in military terms, it was a linear defence that the Serbian security forces tried to put into place in order to stop KLA reinforcement from Albania. So this particular road from Djakovica through Decani to Pec, either side of that there was fierce fighting throughout 1998. And most of the villages along this particular road, Prilep, Decani itself, Gornji Streoc, were destroyed, held by Serbian security forces, and attacked fairly regularly by the KLA that was also in force in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we look at page 3 - and I see it's already displayed in our e-court system - it's page 7 in the B/C/S, there is another heading, this is number 5, which refers to burning houses in Dolovo. Is this -- what you saw in this area similar to the type of destruction of property that you saw in the Decani area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, as I've said already, the -- we were into a series of assaults in various areas where the villages along the major roads were targeted and a huge amount of damage was done to these villages. And this was current throughout most of Kosovo at that particular stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, just referring to this same document I would like to ask you to turn to the last page, this is page 4, and it's a paragraph right under number 9. And in the English this -- in the B/C/S it would be page 9 and it's page 4 in the English. And I would like to direct your attention to a paragraph that starts with: "During our tour we believe that the VJ is giving material support. Vehicles repainted blue, logistics, et cetera." Could you comment on that observation that's made in this report in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I've indicated to the Court, the Pristina Corps, the VJ, had always within based in the province of Kosovo and therefore they had the ability to provide logistic support and that makes eminent sense to use the logistics in place and the various bases that they had quite legally around the area of Kosovo. Several vehicles, mainly armoured personnel carriers, and what we'll call BOV-3s which are primarily designed for anti-aircraft fire, some of these we found to be painted blue over the VJ green. And I would suggest to the Court that normal police operations do not require anti--aircraft and heavy anti-aircraft guns, machine-guns, of 20- 30- and 40-millimetres. These machines were used to blow up or blow down, rather, villages in what I would call stand-off attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how frequently did you see evidence of these sort of machine-guns that had been painted blue and been used by -- in police operations in this manner?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These are mentioned in the many reports that I tendered, and this was common throughout 1998 and into 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you see evidence of that throughout Kosovo, that this sort of equipment was being used in police operations or was this --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- specific to some areas of the province?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, I think it is fair to say it happened throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in your experience, what would be the significance of this - and we're here now talking about the period of end of May 1998 - that you began to see evidence of the VJ giving material support to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I've said, it makes sense that if you've got logistics in place, then you use the logistic capability to further your own operations. It's a different -- or I would suggest it is different when the Vojska Jugoslavije starts to support with both direct fire from tanks and indirect fire from artillery into what is a counter-insurgency operation. This is -- this will inevitably lead to not only a lot more damage but also loss of life from the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to follow-up on that answer, you started about the VJ starting to support with both direct fire and indirect fire. What is the difference between the two, and I'm speaking from the layman perspective. What is the difference between providing direct support and indirect fire support in these operations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In the military, direct fire support is from the likes of a tank or an anti-aircraft armoured personnel carrier firing direct, i.e., line of sight, onto a target; and indirect fire comes from artillery or mortars that can be adjusted on to the relevant targets but they will not usually be line of sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you also said -- in that same answer you said this will inevitably lead to not only a lot more damage but also loss of life from the civilian population. Could you elaborate on that, why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In any counter-insurgency operation there is or there are various levels of force that security forces usually go through the process of using minimum force and then escalating the force required as appropriate. I would suggest that using heavy artillery and anti-aircraft fire onto villages is a very heavy-handed use of fire-power.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I will like to move away from this exhibit, which is 00687, and if you could look at tab 4 of your binder in this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would like to have 00685 displayed up on the screen, and this, again, is a document that's on my list of documents that was handed to the Registry earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see, sir, that this is a report. It's dated 30th July 1998 and follows similar format than the ones we've seen before. And I take it that this report was compiled in a similar fashion than the ones that you have been commenting on so far.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I would like to draw your attention to the paragraph on the first page called "Summary." And if you could look at the second sentence, at the end of the second line it says: "Met assault force of SAJ, PJP and VJ lined up for attack on Malisevo." Was this something you personally observed, these forces lined up to attack Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We had travelled from Orahovac out of the Serbian-held area north towards where we suspected there was a major headquarters of the Kosovo Liberation Army in Malisevo. We were escorted in by the KLA into the KLA headquarters and questioned for some time and then released to travel north up to a village in the area of Lapusnik on the main Pristina-Pec road. It was in that area that we noticed the force as laid down in this report, including tanks, T-55s, and there was a further force west of Lapusnik in the area of Kijevo. And it was quite clear, talking to the commander of this force, that not only were they slightly surprised that we had arrived from Malisevo, his objective, but that it was where they were going once we had got -- left the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you've referred to another force in Kijevo in this report. We see it says that -- it refers to the JSO, PJP, and the VJ being at Kijevo. Here this report refers to the period of end of July 1998. By that time had you observed on the ground any change in the way that the forces deployed on the ground had been operating? And I'm referring specifically to the change of how VJ and MUP forces were operating on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, because it -- at this particular time, as I've reported in several of my other operational reports, that in theory the KLA held about 75 per cent of the area of Kosovo. There are four major routes from -- roughly from west to east across the area of Kosovo. In the north from Mitrovica going west to Klina the road was blocked at Rudnik. Coming south, coming from Pristina through Komorane to Lapusnik, the road from there was also blocked by the KLA. And if you come further south from Pristina down towards Stimlje, the KLA also held that particular road. The only road that was open to the VJ to resupply their western forces was the road that came from Pristina south to Urosevac, and then over the hills down into Prizren which was a very long route and very difficult route because of the mountain passes. I say the KLA controlled it. They had blocked the roads and they had, in military terms, fairly weak positions on the three roads in the north that I've indicated. I think the Serbian security forces - and they will have to answer that question; I can't - they realised that they would have to do something to, if you will, regain control of the area. And therefore, I presume a decision was taken to involve the Vojska Jugoslavije in more of the day-to-day operations. And this culminated in a fairly major push in September/October of 1998, where in effect they did clear these roads. But as in many Balkan conflicts, you clear the area and if you don't remain in the area, the area quickly goes back again under control of the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify your answer, you say that in theory the KLA held about 75 per cent of the area of Kosovo. Are you stating that because of the control of these roads that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It's -- forgive me, it was a very fluid situation. And as I tried to indicate that one side would gain the upper hand and then the other side would decide that it was its turn to gain the upper hand. The KLA did not have the fire-power that the VJ -- or the Serbian security forces could bring to bear, and therefore would use what we call the shoot-and-scoot tactics. There would be a Serbian security reaction, quite rightly, and the situation would go back under Serbian control. But then they would probably withdraw back to their bases and "control" would go back to the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in this specific report that we're looking at we see that there was a joint MUP and VJ assault group preparing to attack Malisevo. Was this the first occasion where you saw that, a joint combined operation, or had you seen that before in other tours of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think this is the first time we'd seen what I referred to as two combat groups, which is roughly company size, 100, 200 people, of both joint forces. And the forces concerned were the VJ with tanks and the MUP with their much better trained areas, the JSO and the SAJ, involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have a question. I know we're supposed to -- we have an unusual sitting time this afternoon and I understand we're breaking at 3.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can go on for a few minutes if that's more convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, sir, and this is page 3 in the B/C/S, page 2 in the English under number 3. It says page 4 and then there's a 3. And it talks about: "The tour turned west on the main road in the direction of Pec ..." Are you there? Do you see that passage in the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And then again it refers to -- the last sentence of that paragraph: "The tour continued west along the main road ..." and it talks about a mixed force of VJ/MUP up to Grebnik VCP." What is VCP, Grebnik VCP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It's a -- what we call a vehicle check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And my question specifically deals with the paragraph which has -- which is referred to as "Comment" and starts with the sentence: "Every village from Lapusnik westward has suffered deliberate damage by cannon and HMG fire. Many houses burning, garages and businesses trashed." If you could comment on that specific observation that's made in the report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It was at this particular stage that when we were touring in Kosovo on more or less a daily basis, we would come across areas that had been destroyed, wantonly destroyed. Generally along the main roads and any villages that in Serbian terminology could harbour KLA. So the statement is as it sounds, every village along that area was damaged. There was daily fires. Corn was set alight. Petrol stations were damaged and any businesses were wrecked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the reference to HMG fire, is that heavy machine-gun fire? Is that what --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. That's correct, heavy machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to the next page. It's page 4 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English. It's a paragraph that starts with "Bravo: Wanton damage," and the sentence -- the first sentence reads: "Every village adjacent to both avenues into Malisevo had suffered severe damage ..." Is this an observation that you made after the attack that was referred to at the start of this report had taken place? Did you return to Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We -- yes, we returned to Malisevo, and as it says in paragraph Charlie, that the Troika group which I took down to Malisevo to show -- show these gentlemen the damage that we were talking about and this was prevalent throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why is it that you did not remain in Malisevo when you saw preparations for an assault on that village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The KLA didn't invite us to stay, but I don't think they would have anyway. But we were asked to leave so we left going north, and we then came into contact with the Serbian security forces, as we've just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the same page towards the bottom there's a paragraph Alpha under "Major questions yet to be answered," and it's at the bottom of page 4 in the B/C/S. And it says: "Loc/number of civpop ..." I take it "civpop" refers to civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And it refers to operations in several villages that are mentioned there and then it says: "Numbers could exceed 100.000 total." Why is this information contained in the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This was part of the assessment of what was becoming displaced persons, internally displaced persons, which was a phrase that we were not allowed to use at that particular time. But it was quite clear that the villagers that had been frightened away from their villages were either living rough or over the border in Albania or actually moved into Crna Gora into Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can stop here because I want to move on to a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that. The court will need to be closed for the witness to leave. We will have the first break now and resume at 3.45. If you wouldn't mind waiting there, Mr. Crosland, until the screens are down and we will resume at 3.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have 00686 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, this is tab 5 in your bundle of documents. If you could have a look at that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have now caught up with all of the documents that have been tendered so far so that as you deal with each new document, if you want to tender it, it will be on the spot, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we see this is a report dated 7th August 1998 and I would like to -- for you to turn to page 2. This is number 2, civpop and wanton destruction. And it's also page 2 in the B/C/S version of the document. In this paragraph there's a reference to: "Throughout entire area very few civpop were seen ..." And if we -- and I'm interested in what is the fourth sentence of this paragraph which starts from: "From Grebnik VCP eastwards to Komorane VCP, villages either side of this road have been completely trashed." If you could comment on that portion of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As we were saying previously, throughout this period in 1998 into the summer and into the autumn area, unfortunately it was very obvious that a very heavy-handed security operation was underway and that all villages along most main roads were destroyed, and even going down the smaller roads in the area one would come across villages that also had been trashed, crops burnt, animals killed, and the -- as I said, the civilian population were nowhere to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you witness this destruction in this specific area referred to in this area in the same way you had in the other areas that we've discussed before in relation to other -- the other reports we've been discussing so far?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. We were more or less in the area on a permanent basis and therefore able to ascertain the ongoing damage virtually day by day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say that all villages along the main roads and specifically I'm interested in this -- what this report refers to, it refers to a specific road, it says all villages have been completely trashed. Approximately how many villages are we speaking about, if you recall, in this --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, I think by the end of the operations in 1998, I'd seen in the region of 2 to 300 villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which had --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That had been damaged in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In this specific report, do you know approximately how many villages it's referring to when it's talking about this axis from Grebnik eastwards, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely, but the major villages along the roadside, all of these had been very heavily damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you have extensive military experience, when we started out you said some 37 years of military experience. Based on your experience, did you -- while you were touring this area and witnessing this sort of damage done to civilian housing and to villages, did you see any sort of military purpose in this destruction or what's been referred to in the various reports we've looked at as wanton destruction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think I've told the Court on several occasions that in a counter-insurgency operation, the security forces have a job to do to maintain security within what was then a sovereign state, Kosovo, part of former Yugoslavia. The manner that they do that, maintain security against what was an increasing threat from the Kosovo Liberation Army, is for them to judge. However, as we have seen and as I've stated on -- in most of my reports, that the wanton damage that took place throughout the whole province of Kosovo cannot have helped the Serbian security forces' plan to look after the local population. And what we saw in increasing numbers was internally displaced persons, IDPs, moving out of their homelands and hiding in various areas, one of which was the Pagarusa valley which is north of the area of Suva Reka. And into this area at various points there was something in the region of probably above a hundred thousand, probably close on 400.000 personnel. It is very difficult to know exact -- the exact numbers. There were also people fleeing westwards into Albania and into Montenegro and southwards into Macedonia. As I've said before, the situation was extremely fluid, but because there was a lack of personnel around and then when the Kosovo Verification Mission came in in, if I remember rightly, October, one of their tasks was to try and ascertain where the IDP, the internally displaced persons, were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify your answer, it says at line 35 -- 25 of the transcript, page 31, it says "probably close to 400.000 personnel." Is that a reference to civilian population or IDPs? Is that what you meant by "personnel"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And going back to my question, I had asked specifically about the purpose -- if you saw any military purpose in what you've referred to as wanton damage throughout the province in -- when these operations were being conducted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. As I've said, I -- if you lose the trust of the civilian population in a military operation, then you have a very difficult job of regaining that trust, and particularly if you've committed huge damage to houses, property, and businesses throughout Kosovo, and this is sadly what happened during 1998 and into 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, going back to the documents in -- just directing your attention to the last paragraph called: "Final comment," and this is also at the end of the document in the B/C/S, it refers to a large MUP convoy seen returning to Pristina with large Serbian flags. Could you comment on this specific section and tell us whether this is something you personally observed, and what you understood was happening when this convoy entered or returned to Pristina on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, as we're aware, throughout the Balkan countries there is a huge rise of nationalism from whichever nationality that happens to be more or less top of the pile. And when it was presumed that the Serbian security forces were starting to regain control, when they returned to their bases on what we would call a rumo [phoen], a turn around of other units taking their places, then quite rightly they were welcomed back for having gone out and done their bit as security forces. And this would take the form of the Serbian flags being waved and small crowds going out to welcome their troops home, which is perfectly understandable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was this something you witnessed yourself on this occasion, what's referred to here in the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, before I move on to the next document, I seek to tender this exhibit, it's 00686, and I understand it's been assigned an exhibit number. I should just mention it. I've been provided the memo by --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has been assigned as P01408, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now moving on to tab 6, this is 00682. This is a report dated 10 September 1998. And, sir, I would like to direct your attention to the bottom of the first page, paragraph 2, which it says: "IDP concentration." I'm just waiting for the document to come up on the screen. And if you could comment on the information that's contained in that paragraph, paragraph 2, which begins with: "IDP concentration between 5 to 15.000 ..."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I mentioned to the Court that the Pagarusa valley, which is some, I suppose, 10 kilometres north of Suva Reka, had been an area into which the villages' IDPs had fled to get out of the way of ongoing military operations. And it -- I think if I remember correctly, it was probably from the Pagarusa valley that these people were now trying to return to rebuild their life back in the various villages that they'd been chased out of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we turn the page we see paragraph 3 to 5 contains some reference to destruction of villages, and then in paragraph 6, did you make an assessment of what lays in store for these people in the coming winter months in that paragraph, paragraph that starts --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This -- sorry. This was of very great concern to the authorities as to how people would get on in the winter, which in Kosovo, as you may well be aware, it can get very cold indeed with snow covering most of the area. And it was something that concerned the Kosovo Verification Mission when they came into the area in October and all the major NGOs, non-governmental organisations, that were there to try and -- or hopefully trying to support the civilian population, whether it be Serb or Albanian was irrelevant, but it was of serious concern that people would be without proper shelter in the forthcoming winter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 7 there's a reference to figures, and a specific figure given there is 171.000 as of the 3rd of September, 1998, of civilian populations. Is this the figure that at the time was the estimate of the number of displaced persons within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I indicated to the Court, the -- to try and get an exact figure was a very difficult science, but it was generally accepted that there were large numbers of person -- of people in Crna Gora, in Montenegro, in Albania, and also in Macedonia as well as internally displaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this specific number would be the number within Kosovo or also included the number of persons who had crossed the border into other countries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I would suspect that this number is within the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, just looking at the bottom of the document we see the name Landsman. Other documents we looked at had the name of Ambassador Donnelly. Could you tell us who Mr. Landsman --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: David Landsman was, Your Honours, the deputy head of mission and in the absence of Ambassador Donnelly would sign the telegraphs, which is very normal procedure within the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you have already explained to the Court how these documents were prepared. I take it that this one which is signed by David Landsman was prepared in a similar fashion as other ones that we have looked at?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I would like to take you to a final document and ask you a question also in relation to a comment you make in your statement. This is 0 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, I seek to tender this document before we move forward, 00682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That has been assigned P01413, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The last tab in your binders, tab 7, 00684. And it's a report dated 6 November 1998 and refers to a conversation you had with General Dimitrijevic, and I'm interested in the second page, if we could turn to paragraph number 5. And this is page 2 both in the English and the B/C/S. Do you recall this meeting in November 1998 with General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall what position General Dimitrijevic held at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic was the head of counter-intelligence, and therefore a very senior member of the Vojska Jugoslavije.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph you say that: "General D did admit that the VJ had overstepped the mark during the summer offensive but also said that the VJ had had to step in in order to salvage the MUP." Now, you've referred to this specific report in this meeting in paragraph 55 and 56 of your statement, and in relation to that specific comment you said in paragraph 55: "He knew that I had personally seen the cooperation between the VJ and the MUP during many operations and was trying to lessen the impact of VJ actions." Could you explain why it is that you understood when he -- when General Dimitrijevic told you -- made this comment to you that he was trying to lessen the impact of VJ actions or -- during the summer offensive?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I've tried to explain to the Court, I'd had many conversations with General Dimitrijevic, General Perisic, and General Krga. General Perisic was Chief of General Staff about to be replaced by General Ojdanic. And General Krga was also head of intelligence. And I suppose because of my experience, one was granted an audience with these three in particular in an attempt to try and help defuse what was a very complex and demanding situation in the area of Kosovo. As I've also said, the Vojska Jugoslavije had stationed in Kosovo Pristina Corps of some 20.000 personnel, and inevitably as the conflict widened they would become involved in an attempt to stop this conflict. Unfortunately, as we've seen, the use of force was excessive. The damage done by the Serbian security forces in toto, as I've stated on many occasions, was also very obvious to anyone that travelled in Kosovo at that particular time. At this stage in November 1998, General Dimitrijevic and General Perisic to an extent had indicated that they were not in the chain of command and that General Pavkovic was reporting direct to President Milosevic, which as the two senior -- or then the two senior VJ officers was an extraordinary situation. As we've also seen throughout the Balkan conflict, that the retaliation by each side as it comes to the top of the pile and gets more powerful than the other side tends to react in a very aggressive way. And sadly, this was true in the province of Kosovo. And hence, I think General Dimitrijevic's comments that inevitably the Vojska Jugoslavije had been dragged into this particular conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say that he was trying to lessen the impact of VJ actions that had occurred, what exactly was he -- did you understand him to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I had made it clear in my reports and I had shown photographic evidence to both General Dimitrijevic and General Perisic of the damage being done and had indicated that this intelligence was now back in various capitals and eventually people would be brought to court to answer for these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you understood his comment to be in relation to that, to the fact that you had drawn his attention to the information you had about what had occurred on the ground during --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, as I've said, by then he appeared not to be in the chain of command and he did not particularly welcome what was going on in Kosovo. But as I've said, it's a very confusing and volatile situation. And as I've said again many times, too much force was used and much too much destruction took place. But I can't answer for the commanders on the spot. They were presumably ordered to carry out these operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I want to now draw your attention back to your statement, and this was tab 1 of your bundle of documents, specifically to events that you witnessed in early 1999. And this is the -- specifically I'm referring to the Racak operation. And you've referred to this in paragraph 67 of your statement, and this is on page 14 of your statement in the English, at the bottom. It's paragraph 67. In paragraph 67, you refer to your first trip into Kosovo in 1999 and you state that that was on 12 January and it lasted until 14th January, and then that you returned on 16th January until 17th January. And you indicate that you were in Kosovo in the aftermath of the Racak incident. Can you just first start by telling us when it is that you heard about what had occurred in Racak in the month of January 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this incident took place just west of a place called Stimlje, which was really the border of Serbian control and going into Kosovo Liberation Army area. And I think if I recall correctly, just before this incident happened three MUP were assassinated on the road coming out of Crnoljevo towards Stimlje. This caused a very major reaction by the Serbian security forces and this was at the time that the Kosovo Verification Mission under Ambassador Walker and General Drewienkiewicz, or DZ as we called him for short, and was probably the straw that broke the camel's back in terms of NATO willingness to try and see this incident through in a peaceful manner. There was a major deployment. I arrived on the afternoon that this incident took place, on the 31st of January [sic], and so the damage had already been done. And I think I actually even recall Ambassador Walker coming back from the area very disappointed, which is a totally inappropriate word, with what had happened and the implications that the Serbian security forces had more or less forced on themselves by carrying out a very heavy-handed operation in retaliation to their personnel being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify the dates. You indicate, and this is at the start of paragraph 67, that you were in Kosovo from the 12th to 14th January and then a second trip on 14th and 7 -- 16th to 17th January, and I see in the transcript we have on the 31st of January. Did you mean to say 31st of January or were you speaking about another date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I apologise, I may have used the wrong date. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe if we just take this one step at a time. You say that your first trip was from 12 to 14th January. Do you recall what was the purpose of that trip, the first trip that you made --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That was just yet another trip down to Kosovo to tour around to gain information, to go and visit the Kosovo Verification Mission which I had briefed and led into Kosovo. So it was a liaison visit as all the other visits had been throughout my time there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you -- during this tour from the 12th to the 14th of January, did you go to the area of Stimlje and the vicinity of the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I -- yes, I think we did. I mean -- I apologise, it's a long time ago and I used to be in and out of this place basically on a daily basis, but it would have been a place to which I would have gone because, as I indicated to the Court, it was the front line between the Serbian forces and the KLA forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 67, and this is on page 15, so it's the middle of paragraph 67 in that -- on that page, it says: "By the amount of troops, both the MUP and -- in all its elements and the VJ were concentrating in that area -- or concentrating that area, it became clear that an operation was about to take place." Did you personally observe this build-up of VJ and MUP elements concentrating in this area or this is some information you received from other sources?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think if I remember correctly it was from both. It would be reports from the Kosovo Verification Mission, whose job it was to monitor the area, and I was down there in order to try and also monitor what was going on. So it would have been joint -- they would have briefed me and I would have gone out on the ground to verify what they had said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in this same paragraph you say that you went -- you returned on the 16th until the 17th and that you were in Kosovo during the aftermath of the Racak incident and visited the scene. Why is it that you visited the scene, you went to Racak village after the incident took place and if you could tell us about what you were able to observe there when you got there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As I've indicated to the Court, Ambassador Walker was extremely angry and concerned that his mission - it's unfair - was able to stop this incident but his mission was clearly there when this incident happened. The consequences of it were quite clear, that NATO could, after an incident of this nature, take appropriate action, whatever that happened to be. General DZ, who I knew well, was also very concerned. And therefore, as part of my job as defence attache to inform my ambassador to make his report back to our government, I went to the area where the problem had been to ascertain for myself that what was being reported was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what were you able to observe there once you arrived to the scene of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult to get close because the Serbian security forces were all over the area, but it was quite clear that a number of people had been killed. And I think if I remember correctly, there were more bodies that were not visible at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you indicate when you're referring to this operation - this is again in paragraph 67 - that it was quite clear that there had been a coordinated move between the VJ and the MUP to clear out the KLA, specifically there was close cooperation between the MUP and the VJ corps based in Pristina under the command of General Lazarevic. Can you explain why it is that you believed that this had been a coordinated action, why you've made this assessment in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In any counter-insurgency operation, as I've stated this afternoon and on other times, it's essential that whatever security forces are being used to carry out what is a very complex operation, that there would be a coordination cell and the obvious place for that would have been in Pristina where both the MUP had a headquarters and the Pristina Corps also had its own headquarters. The reason for coordination is pretty obvious. If you're trying to win a counter-insurgency operation, you need to be able to inform the local population about what is going on. You also need to coordinate the military action between the various elements of your counter-insurgency force; and therefore, I find it extraordinary that the senior people mentioned here, General Pavkovic, Lazarevic, Ojdanic, and Lukic, and Stevanovic, would not have been together masterminding the plan in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this is your own assessment in -- of the situation based on the information you had of how this action took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it's the -- it's -- in the counter-insurgency operations that I've been involved with around the world, it is standard procedure and it makes very -- it makes absolute sense to coordinate your activities both militarily and civilian in trying to help the civilian population, possibly allowing non-governmental organisations in to support the displaced persons. And this inevitably needs to have a coordination centre. So, as I say, in many other areas one has seen a coordination centre as standard -- what we would call standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I have no further questions for this witness. I referred earlier to one of the reports we were looking at, this is 65 ter 00684, and I seek to tender that exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That 65 ter, Your Honours, has already been assigned P01411.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Dobar dan, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It seems that you still speak and understand Serbian well. I'm Veljko Djurdjic, a member of the Defence team of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic, and here with me today is Ms. Marie O'Leary, another team member. I'll try to do something today. Since you have testified before this Tribunal a number of times, I will ask you -- try and ask you what others haven't asked you. Colonel, having read the statements you've given so far, I found out that you graduated from military academy. But with regard to some facts that we learned, I would like to know whether you also had some civilian specialisation. Did you graduate from any civilian faculty; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, I went to what is called prep school and then to public school in England, and then I served as a private soldier before going to Sandhurst, where I was commissioned into my regiment, the parachute regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, am I right in concluding that you were in the infantry and you were also specialised as a paratrooper?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I drew the conclusion from your statements that you graduated from the academy at Sandhurst in 1967; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for two years you served in a military unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to know what you did after these two years of service. What were your positions after that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In the normal run of events I was a junior officer, a lieutenant. I carried out a tour of duty training soldiers in the parachute regiment, and then I went for selection to the special air service and successfully completed selection for that regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were -- are these all of your duties that you had until 1996, when you became military attache in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. I fulfilled a number of appointments as I became more senior, which is a completely normal military career in the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until 1996, did you have any combat experience?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I had many combat experiences around the world in various operational theatres, some of which are of a classified nature and I am not entitled to tell this Court of those particular operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, is there any unclassified information that you could share with this Tribunal for us to know more about your combat experience? And one more thing, did the British government waive your right to keep military secrets or didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can tell you, Your Honours, about experiences in Northern Ireland, in the Middle East, other areas are classified to the UK government and I'm not at -- I'm not allowed to speak about those other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this because at the end of your answers that you gave to the OTP you said that throughout the world you took part in security operations and that you have much experience and that you know that there is always a coordination centre. I'm not asking questions about your positions or duties that you -- while performing intelligence work. I'm exclusively interested in your combat experience as an infantry officer or a paratrooper if you took part in military operations conducted either by your country, the UK, or by NATO. Of course, I'm not interested in classified operations or security operations of other types.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I can repeat, I've been involved in operations in Northern Ireland. I've been involved in operations in the Middle East. I took part in the Falklands war, and I was observing operations in Kosovo from 1996 to 1999, and I went back in with KFOR as an observer or liaison officer, rather, to General Mike Jackson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you the following: As a military attache of Great Britain, were you staff of the UK embassy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we were accredited staff to our embassy in Belgrade, and more importantly, we were also accredited through the FLS, the Foreign Liaison Service, to the Vojska Jugoslavije. And on the start of my tour of duty there, I was officially presented to General Perisic, who was then the Chief of the General Staff, which is as normal procedure on any defence attache joining a post in another -- in a host country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a layman when it comes to these issues, but I would like to know, were you sent to the British embassy in Belgrade as a Foreign Office staff or a staff of some other ministry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. All our defence attaches or military attaches are posted to host nations from the Ministry of Defence and attached to their individual embassies for a tour of duty that can be two years, three years, or sometimes longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now what I would like to know, did you as defence attache have your own personnel that worked on the issues you dealt with; and if so, how many personnel did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I had one senior warrant officer and he -- personal assistant, and that was the sum total of my staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
